Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/feature-stories/trial-fire-look-nist-fire-testing-through-years Credit: © Earl Zubkoff Trial by Fire: A Look at NIST Fire Testing Through the Years March 6, 2018 Facebook Linkedin X.com Email Fire testing may have started some 2.5 million years ago when one of our ancestors stuck his hand into the first flame and “scientifically” determined that the temperature was too hot to bear. Since that primitive beginning, humans have been on an unending quest to understand, measure and exploit the behavior of fire — and most importantly, to improve our ability to protect life and property from its ravages. Fire testing at NIST, a staple of the agency’s research since the early 1900s, has helped provide much of the data, insights and knowledge demanded by that pursuit. Find out more about NIST's fire research and the National Fire Research Laboratory . Credit: NIST Digital Archives NIST conducted what may have been America’s first full-scale fire test when researchers burned down two condemned buildings in Washington, D.C., on June 17, 1928. Data from this experiment, along with previous work by pioneer fire researcher Simon H. Ingberg, eventually led to uniform fire resistance standards for buildings.

Trouble Funk: Tiny Desk Concert May 30, 2018 12:00 PM ET By Abby O'Neill Credit: NPR Go-go — Washington D.C.'s regional twist on funk — reigned in the DMV during the 1980s, and one of the scene's signature acts was Trouble Funk. More than 30 years later, the collective, led by Big Tony Fisher, still fills sold-out venues with heavyweight percussion and call-and-response lyrics. Trouble Funk concerts are bona fide jam sessions, so I was determined to squeeze their unrelenting rhythms behind the Tiny Desk. With 12 members sandwiched into a cramped space, the electricity was almost tangible as they launched into the 1982 banger "Pump Me Up," a song sampled in Public Enemy's protest anthem "Fight the Power" and M/A/R/R/S's dance classic "Pump Up The Volume." The drum breaks here are definitive go-go and it was hard to discern who was having more fun: the band or the audience. In the Philippines, where he attended the Asean Summit, Trump nodded when asked by a journalist about the report that Tehran was planning to detonate a so-called dirty bomb in the US capital and said: "We're looking into it." CNN cited unnamed US intelligence officials suggesting Iran could target senior figures in Trump's administration with such an attack. Iran called the claim "baseless." Concerns about dirty bombs grew after the 9/11 attacks in 2001, although no such attack has ever occurred. Such a device would contain radioactive material - such as uranium - which would be scattered through the air when its conventional explosive detonated. The BBC has not independently verified CNN's reporting. During his comments to reporters in Manila, Trump was asked whether there was reason to believe an attack was imminent. TSCA Section 21 Under TSCA section 21, any person may petition EPA to initiate a proceeding for the issuance, amendment, or repeal of a rule or order under: Section 4 -- rules or orders requiring chemical testing; Section 6 -- rules imposing regulatory controls on chemicals; Section 8 -- rules requiring information; or Section 5(e) or (f) -- orders affecting new chemical substances. The petition must be filed in EPA's Office of the Administrator and set forth the facts that are claimed to establish the necessity for the action requested. EPA is required to grant or deny the petition within 90 days from the day the petition is filed with EPA. If EPA grants the petition, EPA must promptly commence an appropriate proceeding. If EPA denies the petition, the reasons for denial must be published in the Federal Register. Обозначение обособленной велосипедной дорожки: highway=cycleway - основной тег линии, который указывает, что путь предназначен для движения на велосипедах. foot=no - явно запрещает движение пешеходов (если пешеходам запрещено находиться на этой дорожке). Если пешеходы разрешены, но дорожка разделена на зоны, используют foot=yes и segregated=yes/no . Велосипедная дорожка + тротуар: Комбинация тэгов для обозначения пешеходного тротуара, совмещённого с выделенной велосипедной дорожкой, которая конструктивно или визуально отделена от пешеходной зоны: highway=footway - обозначает, что данный объект является обустроенной дорожкой, предназначенной в первую очередь для пешеходов. footway=sidewalk - уточняет тип пешеходной дорожки. Этот тег указывает, что дорожка является тротуаром, то есть идет параллельно автомобильной дороге (обычно повторяя её геометрию). bicycle=designated - указывает на официальный юридический статус для велосипедистов. Это значит, что дорожка специально выделена/предназначена для движения на велосипеде (например, установлен соответствующий знак или нанесена разметка), а не просто «разрешена для транзита». segregated=yes - означает, что потоки пешеходов и велосипедистов разделены. pages.description: Long thought to have been looted from northern England by Scottish tribes, the larger-than-life leg may have actually been displayed in Roman Scotland, before it was carefully dismantled and buried by retreating forces
pages.text: Two Centuries After This Bronze Leg Emerged From a Scottish Bog, Archaeologists Believe It May Have Belonged to a Towering Statue of a Roman Emperor on Horseback Skip to main content Curator Fraser Hunter examines the bronze leg. Duncan McGlynn In 1820, a larger-than-life gilded bronze lower leg was pulled out of a bog in the Scottish Borders region. For more than two centuries, historians discredited the idea that the Roman-era artifact came from Scotland, instead assuming that it was hacked off a monument in England and hauled north by marauding tribes. But ahead of “ Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire ,” an exhibition at the National Museum of Scotland (NMS), researchers have determined that the so-called “Milsington leg” was not stolen from the south, nor was it violently severed. Instead, they posit that it formed part of a colossal equestrian statue of the Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius that once stood in southern Scotland in the second century C.E., before it was dismantled by retreating Roman troops. “This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome’s second attempt at conquering Scotland,” Fraser Hunter , principal curator of prehistoric and Roman archaeology at NMS, says in a statement . The bronze leg shows no signs of being violently hacked off the larger statue. From late Thursday to early Saturday, the typhoon battered Taiwan and Japan’s southern islands. Champi approached the east coast of Taiwan before the centre of the storm turned south along the Yilan County coastline, looping offshore and then tracking northwards away from the island. The storm brought gusts of up to 141mph and 48-hour rainfall totals of more than 620mm to parts of Yilan. So far, the death toll remains at one, with 527 reported injured. There were widespread power outages, with more than 288,000 houses having no electricity at one point, although most had since been reconnected. With a massive body, sharp teeth, and jaws so powerful they could crush a car, this famous carnivore dominated the forested river valleys in western North America during the late Cretaceous period, 68 million years ago. Although T. rex is a household name, what we know about this tyrannosaur is constantly evolving. Improved technologies, such as biomechanical modeling and x-ray imaging, have allowed scientists to gain a deeper understanding of how this apex predator lived. Strengths Tyrannosaurus rex , whose name means “ king of the tyrant lizards ,” was built to rule. This dinosaur’s muscular body stretched as long as 40 feet—about the size of a school bus —from its snout to the tip of its powerful tail. Weighing up to eight tons, T. rex stomped headfirst across its territory on two strong legs. U.S. Gridded Methane Emissions The gridded EPA U.S. methane greenhouse gas inventory (gridded methane GHGI) includes time series of annual methane emission maps with 0.1° x 0.1° (~ 10 x 10 km) spatial and monthly temporal resolution for the contiguous United States (CONUS). This gridded methane inventory is designed to be consistent with methane emissions from the U.S. EPA Inventory of U.S. Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Sinks (U.S. GHGI). The gridded methane GHGI dataset includes annual methane emission fluxes for over 25 inventory emission source categories, including those from agriculture, petroleum and natural gas systems, coal mining, and waste. Gridded methane emissions data are generated by allocating national annual U.S. GHGI methane emissions from individual source categories to a 0.1° x 0.1° CONUS grid, using a series of spatial and temporal 'proxy' datasets at the state, county, and grid levels. Where possible, proxy data are the same data used to develop the U.S. GHGI so that the gridded emissions can be, as closely as possible, a spatial and temporal representation of the national-level U.S. GHGI. Hanacek/NIST Over the last century, building codes and standards in the U.S. have been improved to better protect people from harm. But what triggered these updates? And how are decisions made about what to change? The short answer: When buildings fail to keep their occupants safe or even come close to failing during a catastrophic event — natural, human-caused or a mix of both — organizations step up to study what caused the failure. Then, government and industry organizations take action through established processes to etch those lessons into codes. As an agency that has studied and investigated building failures for more than 50 years and wields legislative authority to get to the bottom of disasters, NIST plays a key role in updating codes. In addition to calling for enhanced codes and standards based on technical findings, NIST experts, along with many others, work to turn these recommendations into actionable codes. pages.text: Understanding Geographic Identifiers (GEOIDs) Understanding Geographic Identifiers (GEOIDs) Skip Navigation Within Guidance for Geography Users Understanding Geographic Identifiers (GEOIDs) What are GEOIDs? The Census Bureau and other state and federal agencies are responsible for assigning geographic identifiers, or GEOIDs, to geographic entities to facilitate the organization, presentation, and exchange of geographic and statistical data. GEOIDs are numeric codes that uniquely identify all administrative/legal and statistical geographic areas for which the Census Bureau tabulates data. From Alaska, the largest state, to the smallest census block in New York City, every geographic area has a unique GEOID. Some of the most common administrative/legal and statistical geographic entities with unique GEOIDs include states, counties, congressional districts, core based statistical areas (metropolitan and micropolitan areas), census tracts, block groups and census blocks. Why Are GEOIDs Important? GEOIDs are very important for understanding and interpreting geographic and demographic data and their relationship to one another. Data users rely on GEOIDs to join the appropriate demographic data from censuses and surveys, such as the American Community Survey (ACS), to various levels of geography for data analysis, interpretation and mapping. The key principles of UD are simplicity, flexibility, and efficiency. Whether we realize it or not, most of us benefit from UD on a daily basis. Originally developed in response to the needs of the aging population and people with disabilities, UD now increases access to products, places, and services for all populations. Companies that embrace UD in their facilities, programs, and services recognize that their workforce and customers have a broad range of abilities, ages, reading levels, learning styles, languages, etc.—and an even wider variety of needs and expectations. Good customer service means providing every customer with a welcoming environment, respectful treatment, and needed information. This goes for the workforce as well. UD provides an important tool set for companies seeking to provide such advantages for both their customers and their employees.
